opus-5.5.text:
So, when you look at what language actually did for us as a species, I think it comes down to two things.

The first is that language lets you take what's in your head and put it into someone else's head. Before language, if I learned that a certain berry was poisonous, the only way you'd learn it was by watching me get sick, or getting sick yourself. With language, I can just tell you. Knowledge stops dying with the individual. It accumulates. One person discovers fire, and a thousand years later a kid can learn about it in a sentence without reinventing it. That's an enormous shortcut, and it's why we stand on the shoulders of everyone who came before us.

The second superpower, the one I find more fascinating, is that language lets us talk about things that don't exist. Other animals communicate. A monkey can make a call that means "there's a snake." But as far as we know, no monkey can say "imagine there's a snake," or "tomorrow there might be a snake," or "the snake spirit will protect you if you behave." Language lets us describe the future, the hypothetical, the imaginary. And once you can do that, you can create shared fictions: money, nations, laws, religions, companies. None of these exist physically. They exist because millions of us agree to believe in them, and language is the glue that makes that agreement possible.

Put those two together and you get something no other species has. You can transmit knowledge across generations, and you can coordinate huge numbers of strangers around ideas that only live in our minds. That's what lets humans cooperate at a scale of millions, not just within a small tribe.

And from a neuroscience perspective, what's interesting is that the brain wasn't really built for this. We repurposed machinery that evolved for other things. Language is a kind of hack on top of the brain, and that hack changed everything about how we live.

r001.rationale: The response describes telling another person and coordinating millions around shared ideas, but does not clearly say language broadcasts information to a large audience.

r002.rationale: It says knowledge accumulates and can be transmitted across generations, so later people can learn without rediscovering it.

r003.rationale: It says language lets people discuss things that do not exist and create shared fictions that live in people’s minds.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it, language did two things for us that no other species really got, and they're kind of mirror images of each other.

The first one is that it let us share what's in our head with someone else without them having to live through it. Before language, if I learned that a certain berry kills you, the only way you learn it is you watch me die, or you eat the berry. Suddenly I can just tell you. I can compress an entire experience into a few sounds and transplant it into your brain. That's the first superpower, this ability to move knowledge between minds. And it compounds. You tell two people, they tell two people, and now the whole tribe knows something nobody in the tribe had to actually experience. That's essentially how culture starts. It's why we don't start from zero every generation.

The second one is more subtle, and I think it's actually the bigger one. Language let us talk about things that don't exist. Not just "there's a lion behind that rock" but "there's a god who lives in that rock," or "this piece of paper is worth a cow," or "tomorrow we're going to go hunt." Once you can name something that isn't in front of you, you can plan, you can imagine, you can coordinate around a fiction. Money is a fiction. Nations are fictions. A company is a fiction. None of it is real in the way a rock is real, but because we can all say the word and agree on it, we can get thousands of strangers to cooperate. No chimp is going to work with a chimp it's never met because they both believe in the same corporation.

And what's interesting from the brain side is that these two things, sharing experience and inventing the unreal, actually come from the same machinery. The moment you have a symbol that stands for a thing, you've already detached the symbol from the thing. So the price of being able to tell you about the berry is that I can also lie to you about the berry. The same tool that gives you science gives you religion, and propaganda, and Bitcoin. It's the same superpower, just pointed in different directions.

r001.rationale: It says one person can tell others about an experience and that the knowledge can spread until the whole tribe knows it.

r002.rationale: It says accumulated knowledge is why people “don’t start from zero every generation,” clearly describing preservation across generations.

r003.rationale: It explains that language lets people talk about things that do not exist, then agree on shared fictions such as money or nations.

astra-6.text:
I think language gave us two extraordinary abilities. One is to learn from experiences we didn’t have. You discover something, you tell me, and now I can benefit from that knowledge without having to repeat your experiment—or make your mistake. And that knowledge can accumulate across generations.

The second is to share things that don’t exist yet, or that exist only in our imagination. I can describe a possible future, and suddenly we can both work toward it. We can create stories, rules, institutions—things that allow enormous numbers of people who have never met to cooperate. So we’re no longer limited to our own experience or to what’s immediately in front of us.

r001.rationale: It says language lets people share stories, rules, and institutions so that enormous numbers of people who have never met can cooperate, conveying information reaching a large audience.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says knowledge can accumulate across generations.

r003.rationale: It describes sharing things that do not yet exist or exist only in imagination.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language gave us two superpowers. One is the ability to learn from experiences we never had. You touch fire and get burned, and you can tell me, “Don’t touch that.” Now I get the benefit of your experience without paying the price. And we can do that across generations, so every person doesn’t have to figure everything out from scratch.

The second is the ability to talk about things that don’t exist—at least not yet. We can describe a possible future, get other people to imagine it with us, and then work together to make it happen. We’re no longer limited to reacting to what’s in front of us. We can agree on something in our heads and organize our behavior around it.

r001.rationale: It describes telling another person and sharing experience, but does not say language lets information reach large audiences.

r002.rationale: It says people can share experience across generations so each person does not have to start from scratch.

r003.rationale: It says people can describe possible futures that do not yet exist and get others to imagine them together.
